en: And I lie here telling my sorrow!
The sable cap upon one’s head—
My beloved colt,
Who has not worn one at a jaunty tilt?
While pride remained upon our heads,
Who did not live in delight?
When they saw your uncle,
No khan of China failed to panic.
Yesterday, when he assembled the Muslim giants,
When we brought hell down upon
Beijing, beyond the reach of the flood,
And exacted its reckoning,
Why did I not meet the decree
God had ordained at that time?
While my companion was alive,
Why did I not die then!
Black-sooted and bulletproof—
This is the place where we donned it;
This is the place where I fought
Kongurbai, khan of the Chinese!
We stood out in single combat,
And your capable uncle Bakai
Fought without rest for seven days,
Toppling their mighty men
And spearing them down from the cliff!
Renowned China-Kakanchin,
My dear foal,
Is a people left behind by wretched me!
This is where I faced khans
Clad in berenji armor;
This is where I fought apart
Against the Chinese people,
Clad in five-layered waistcoats and blue coats!
Making my horse dance in single combat,
This is the place where I went;
Many a marvelous wonder—
This is the place where I wrought it.
The road to Beijing divides five ways—
I told you that earlier!
The road to Beijing has five branches.
There, where the mist parts,
Where something massive appears,
There, where the mountain summit protrudes,
Where the eagle's peak rises sheer,
For the numerous Chinese-Kakan people,
That is the mine where they dig gold,
The place where they find their wealth!
The tribes who inhabit that land
Are the Solon and the many Shibe—
They are two peoples.
I took much tribute from them in gold;
Bakai was their overlord!
Into the midst of those people,
My stride carried me;
While my generous lord was alive,
I firmly exacted tribute from that people!
There, where the dark hills divide,
Where their peaks appear arched,
That is rugged Kara-Too.
That is the mine from which tea is taken;
When I had the power,
I was the one who exacted tribute in tea!
That is the very border;
That is where the troops stood!
When its jang-jun issued a decree,
That flood would surge over everything!
It is a land my bloodthirsty hero conquered,
A place where the Muslims
Were sated with abundant wealth!
Fair-faced young wives and beautiful girls—
A place where we could not gather them all as spoils,
A place whose gold and silver
None could finish loading!
That rising ridge ahead
Is the land of No Return;
Anyone who encountered it met his death—
Such are those woeful Chinese people!
While my fortune remained whole,
While my bloodthirsty hero lived,
It was a place where we brought turmoil,
Where we clashed and fought,
Where many lives were lost,
And where we took their khanate!
Then my wings had not yet been scorched;
My forearms were thick and thundering,
And I killed whoever I encountered,
Roaming at will!
Not merely China, but the age itself,
Accursed world,
Was then under my dominion!
Those pale hills and burning dust—
That is the road of No Return!
Where the hills rise jagged,
That is the Chok-Tabylgy Pass!
At Chok-Tabylgy dwells
Where the great black horse is tethered,
That infidel, son of the kalday,
Hero Khan Kongurbai—
That is where he himself lies encamped!
That blue-gray narrow gorge
Is where the accursed infidel
Placed his magic!
Within that very enchantment,
I have heard that Beijing's magic
Turned its face elsewhere,
And that they fortified it
Five times more strongly than before!
Within that very enchantment,
In the place they excavated,
Upon the road where they set the magic,
No mortal has traveled;
No challenger remained alive.
Upon that very road
There are sorcerers and a khan;
Among the smooth-skinned swine
There are predators of every kind!
Its tiger bore fifteen cubs;
No mortal ventured near!
There are sixty dragons,
And beyond them
A creature held there by magic:
There is a sword-snouted elephant.
Beijing is no easy road;
My precious son, understand!
Among those seething infidels,
How many places have a khan;
There are countless kinds of enchantments
That speak in human tongues,
And there are guardians too.
There is a beast beyond words,
There is a pass on which they set their resolve,
There is a place where they lie entrenched!
It has a road mortals long to see,
And a ditch beside the road
Where the ignorant fall and die!
It has boiling brine
Into which the ignorant plunge and die;
There is an iron-cable net
That traps those who go reconnoitering.
Those who go there never turn back—
Such are those calamitous Chinese people!
I am the Bakai who demanded Beijing's tribute
And took it!
The place where I passed through and ruled
Has become a wretched land left by Manas!
Blue haze and low mist—
That is the pass of Kaspang-Too!
The haze beyond the reach of sight—
That is the Sary-Suu of Kürpüldök,
That is the bank of the Sary-Suu!
If my young hero remains safe,
Those are the Chinese people he will fight;
I am the Bakai who saw them
In the days of sacred power!
If we ride onward from here,
That is the pale, pebbled pass;
That is where Kongurbai's Kuukulja
Lies on watch!
Yesterday, when Alman struck Kakan,
When your Ala shot
The wild ram standing guard,
That accursed Kuukulja
Fell into terrible rage
And left behind its young.
Its young grew up
And, they say, reached seven years of age;
That Akkulja, all by itself—
That swine, ablaze with rage—
Became the guardian of the land, they say.
I hear it is the chief guardian
Of hero Kongurbai,
Whose tent poles are gold!
Orphaned and grown,
I heard it rose for no good purpose;
I heard this wild ram
Surpassed the former ram.
There lies the Kara-Kyya side;
Ah, my dear foal,
Curse the ram and all with it—
This is the dark hour!
If we shoot and slaughter that wild ram,
And feast upon its fatty meat,
It will be God's gift to us!
We shall scatter Kongurbai's livestock
And raid the accursed one's horses,
Fleeing with them from Keng-Shor!
If the wild ram escapes,
We shall see grievous trouble
And die fighting
Against that accursed swine!
The Chinese are forty tribes;
My mighty son, hear this!
Beijing is no worthless land,
And Alööke's Kongurbai
Is no hero who avoids a confrontation!
The renowned Kongurbai
Is the defender of this Beijing!
This is the building set upon Kerüü;
This is the mighty khan of the monks,
The hero who deceived
Your father Manas six times!
He himself must now have a blue-gray beard.
Kongurbai is no easy foe,
A slave more skillful than a spearman,
A mighty slave who knows
The enemy's stratagems exceedingly well.
That is the prominent building on the pass;
That corrupt, accursed man
Is the mighty khan of Beijing!
My dear foal,
Your wretched uncle Bakai
Will tell you much
About the exceptionally cunning Kalcha!
You halted your accursed uncle Bakai
In an empty ravine,
Brought his feats of valor to mind,
And made him lament hardship today!
In Bakai's old age,
Sorrow comes to mind:
With golden collar and copper sleeves,
A double coat of ring mail with larklike eyes,
A netted outer garment and a wide coat—
When worn in battle, no bullet pierced it;
It was the armor I used to wear.
Mounted on a tulpar and gripping a banner,
While my falcon Manas lived,
It was the road I used to travel!”
Your accursed uncle Bakai,
Your elder like a prophet,
Took the road he himself had seen,
Along valleys with springs and streams.
Uncle Bakai, the dear hero,
The dear warrior, reconnoitered,
Crossing uneven ground.
Kökcholok beneath him
Flickered his two legs;
When Kökcholok traveled,
The tips of the grasses trembled.
Tulpar above all, Kökcholok—
When capable Bakai cried, “Chu!”
No livestock could match his walking pace,
And no wind could match his trot.
His broad rump rolled,
The swift pacer flashed,
And when he opened his mouth, he snorted;
The black earth, hard as a kiln,
Burst apart beneath his hooves.
He did not tire when reconnoitering;
Your uncle Bakai's tulpar
Shone upon the road!
Semetey's falcon,
From his father, gray-wolf Manas,
Your young hero was born to surpass him;
His opponent was Kongurbai,
And he had come to Beijing.
He who dwelt in Middle Keng-Kol
